title: Marketplace v2 SKU packaging notes (working) — base vs add-ons, discount constraints, Sales alignment
content:
Context
- This is a working doc to capture packaging tradeoffs for the marketplace refresh (AWS + GCP).
- Goal: make SKUs understandable to buyers + pass marketplace review + map cleanly to Redwood entitlements + remain quoteable by Sales.
- Not a final pricing doc; focus is “what is base vs add-on” and “what can/can’t we discount in marketplace mechanics”.

Guiding principles (v2)
1) Marketplace SKUs should map 1:1 to a small set of internal plan codes + explicit add-on entitlements. Avoid “mystery bundles”.
2) Base SKUs should be useful out of the box for self-serve procurement + POC. Add-ons should unlock procurement/compliance extras and premium ops commitments.
3) Keep the add-on list short and defensible. If we can’t reliably provision/measure/support it, it shouldn’t be its own line item.
4) Don’t build a parallel pricing universe in marketplace. Same naming, same core feature boundaries as Console/billing.
5) Discounting should primarily happen via Private Offers (AWS) / Private Offers (GCP) rather than trying to represent discounts as credits or “free months” in listing text.

SKU taxonomy (current draft)
A) Hosted API (usage-based)
- Base: “Redwood Inference — Hosted API”
  - Includes: API access (chat/text/embeddings/rerank as applicable to catalog), standard rate limits, standard support, basic usage analytics.
  - Meter: tokens/embedding units (internal: hosted_api meters).
  - Regions: where hosted is available.
- Add-ons (candidate list)
  1) “Compliance Pack” (see definition below)
  2) “Extended Observability Retention” (if we can implement as an entitlement w/ clear retention periods)
  3) “Premium SLA” (if we can enforce/track: uptime/latency SLO + response times)

B) Dedicated (reserved capacity)
- Base: “Redwood Inference — Dedicated Capacity”
  - Includes: reserved GPU pool, data isolation at the tenant level, configurable autoscaling policy within reserved pool, standard onboarding support.
  - Meter/commit: monthly commit / hourly capacity dimension (depends on marketplace constraints; see notes below).
- Add-ons (candidate list)
  1) “Burst Capacity” (only if we can cleanly scope: e.g., burst-to-hosted or burst-to-shared dedicated pool; avoid complicated policy in v2)
  2) “Premium SLA” (more relevant than Hosted; buyers ask for it)
  3) “Compliance Pack” (audit logging + controls language; esp regulated)

C) Private (VPC / on-prem)
- Base: “Redwood Inference — Private Deployment”
  - Includes: private control plane option, customer-managed networking, baseline audit logging hooks, standard deployment support.
  - Packaging caution: marketplace buyers expect a deployable artifact (AMI / Helm / Terraform) + clear shared responsibility model.
- Add-ons
  1) “Compliance Pack”
  2) “Premium SLA / Enterprise Support” (naming tbd; must match Legal’s term set)
  3) “On-Prem Connector / Air-gapped Support” (ONLY if we are willing to operationalize; otherwise keep as “contact sales” and handle via direct contract)

Definition proposals (base vs add-on)

1) Compliance Pack (proposed as a single add-on across Hosted/Dedicated/Private)
What it IS (things we can consistently stand behind)
- Customer-facing security documentation bundle + procurement readiness:
  - Access to SOC 2 report via NDA process (not “included in listing” but entitlement can grant access path)
  - Security packet artifacts (encryption overview, audit logging overview, shared responsibility summary)
- Product controls (must be real entitlements / config)
  - Extended audit log access/exports (where available) OR “audit log export enablement” if we gate by entitlement
  - Configurable data retention controls (if implemented). If not implemented, do not claim “configurable retention” as part of the pack.
- Support workflow
  - Security questionnaire handling SLA (e.g., 5 business days) — check with Security/GRC if we can commit.

What it is NOT (avoid overpromising)
- Not a guarantee of compliance (no “HIPAA compliant” / “FedRAMP ready” language unless explicitly approved).
- Not a promise of specific certifications beyond what we have today (must align with Olga/Aisha sign-off).
- Not “customer-managed keys” unless Private actually supports it end-to-end in stated environments.

Open question
- Does Compliance Pack need to be split (Audit Logging vs Evidence Access vs Retention)? My take: keep it single in v2 to reduce SKU explosion.
- If Retention requires significant engineering or introduces a lot of edge cases, make Retention its own add-on later, not in v2.

2) Extended Observability Retention (add-on)
- Base includes: basic dashboards + standard retention (e.g., 7/14/30 days — we need to pick and ensure it matches actual Console behavior).
- Add-on includes: extended retention (e.g., 90/180/365) + export APIs.
- Packaging concern: if the only difference is “we will keep data longer”, marketplace reviewers may ask for precise terms. We must match what the product actually does.

3) Premium SLA (add-on)
- Base includes: standard support + “best effort” response.
- Premium SLA includes:
  - Uptime target (e.g., 99.9%) and response times
  - Potentially latency SLO for Dedicated only (careful on Hosted; too many workload variables)
- Packaging concern: SLA language must be consistent with Legal terms; marketplace listing copy must not contradict the MSA/SLA doc.

Discounting + marketplace mechanics (constraints)

General
- Most marketplace discounting is easiest/cleanest via Private Offers rather than trying to list “discounted SKU” publicly.
- Avoid “credits” language in marketplace. Finance has flagged revrec + marketplace fee complications (see fees/revrec sensitivity analysis).

AWS Marketplace notes (from Sales/Finance threads; validate with Partnerships)
- Private Offers are the primary way to do enterprise discounting / commits.
- Public listing prices should be the guardrail prices (floor-ish) to avoid channel conflict.
- Metered usage SKUs: be careful with lots of dimensions. Token meters should be simple and map to our internal meters 1:1.
- Enterprise asks we cannot do cleanly in AWS Marketplace:
  - Highly custom contract terms (route to direct contract)
  - Non-standard payment schedules beyond what AWS supports
  - Complex bundled discounts across multiple products (Hosted + Dedicated + Private + add-ons) — may be possible but operationally messy.

GCP Marketplace notes (validate)
- Private offers exist but deal structures differ.
- GCP reviewers are strict on solution description matching what is actually provisioned.
- If a SKU requires human-led provisioning (Dedicated/Private), we must be clear in steps and set expectations.

Where we should draw the line: marketplace vs direct contract
- Push marketplace when:
  - Customer requires committed spend through cloud provider
  - Standard product terms are acceptable
  - Discount is within pre-approved bands (Finance/Sales policy)
- Push direct contract when:
  - Customer demands material term changes (indemnity, liability caps, DPA custom, bespoke security addenda)
  - Discounting goes beyond private offer guardrails / needs multi-product netting that Finance can’t support cleanly
  - On-prem/air-gapped deployments requiring custom SOW

Alignment with Sales quoting / internal systems

Naming conventions
- Keep SKU names consistent across:
  - Marketplace listing title
  - Redwood Console plan display name
  - Internal billing plan codes
  - Sales collateral (deck + one-pagers)
- Avoid environment-specific suffixes in customer-facing names when possible (e.g., don’t make buyers parse “hosted-prod-us” SKUs).

Entitlements and plan codes (high-level mapping)
- Each base SKU should map to a single internal base plan code:
  - hosted_api_base
  - dedicated_base
  - private_base
- Add-ons map to additive entitlements:
  - addon_compliance_pack
  - addon_obs_retention_XXX
  - addon_premium_sla
- Requirement for Engineering (Cole/Ethan): the mapping layer must support multiple add-ons stacked + upgrades/downgrades (see PM-876).

Sales quote workflow (what we need to make easy)
- AEs should be able to say:
  1) “Pick your deployment model (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)”
  2) “Add Compliance Pack / Premium SLA if you need it”
  3) “We’ll send a private offer via your cloud marketplace account ID(s)”
- SE/CS should be able to validate purchase -> entitlement -> org linking within 1–2 steps in Console.

Common friction points to design around
- Customers buying add-ons without base SKU (we should prevent or make it a no-op with clear error).
- Multiple cloud accounts buying for one Redwood org (need clear linking policy).
- Region mismatch: buyer purchases in one region but expects provisioning elsewhere (Dedicated/Private especially).

Open questions / decisions needed
1) Do we allow Compliance Pack to be purchased for Hosted only, or require it to be tied to an org (works across Hosted + Dedicated)?
   - Preference: tie to org; entitlement is global. But marketplaces may force per-product attachment. Need to confirm.
2) Observability retention: can we commit to exact retention durations by entitlement at launch?
   - If not, remove from v2 SKU list and treat as “roadmap / contact sales”.
3) Premium SLA packaging: single add-on across all offerings vs Dedicated/Private only.
   - My take: offer for Dedicated + Private first; keep Hosted language minimal.
4) Dedicated burst: is this a real separately controlled capability or just “we’ll work with you”? If the latter, keep out of marketplace SKUs.

Action items
- Soojin: confirm final customer-facing naming and copy boundaries for Compliance Pack + Premium SLA (ensure no overclaims).
- Naomi + Marcus/Olga: sanity check compliance pack definition vs what we can safely claim in listings + FAQ.
- Laura (Finance): provide final discount guardrails for marketplace private offers (bands, floor pricing guidance) + how to message internally.
- Cole (Billing): confirm plan code + entitlement model supports stacking add-ons + upgrade/downgrade semantics.
- Markus (SE): review for field usability (can an AE explain this in 60 seconds?).

Notes to self / backlog
- Keep an eye on marketplace reviewer feedback: they tend to push back on vague “enterprise-grade” claims and want concrete deployment steps.
- Don’t let add-ons become “everything we don’t want to include in base”. If it’s essential for a successful POC, it should be base.
- We should align the final SKU table with the marketplace onboarding docs so the terminology matches exactly (otherwise Support gets crushed post-launch).
